messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Margaret is a 55-year-old American woman, a Catholic nun who has lived for many years in a convent attached to a parish school. She speaks about the worst day of her life with an unsettling combination of precision and rupture: some parts arrive with unbearable sharpness, while others seem to drop away entirely. The trauma was not something done to her body, but something she witnessed happening to someone she loved and believed she should have kept safe. She had been very close to one of the younger sisters in her community, a woman she had helped mentor after final vows. On the day of the event, the two of them had gone together off church grounds for an ordinary errand. Margaret remembers the light, the sound of traffic, the bag in the other sister’s hand, and the instant the scene changed. She can describe particular details with exactness—the angle of her companion’s body, the look on her face, the sickening awareness that something irreversible had happened—but when she tries to recount the next several moments, there are blanks she cannot fill. She knows she moved, called out, and tried to help, but the sequence is broken. What remains intact is the conviction that she did not do what she should have done.

In the months after the death, Margaret returned to the convent and resumed the visible shape of religious life, but internally her days narrowed. She had come to believe the event happened because of the way she acted that day. If she had suggested a different route, if she had walked on the other side, if she had been more alert, if she had somehow anticipated danger, then the other sister might still be alive. She says this not as speculation but with the certainty of a moral verdict. More than once in session she has said, quietly and without drama, that she failed to protect her. Alongside this is a more global loss of confidence in herself. Decisions that once felt ordinary—leading prayer, accompanying a novice, organizing errands—now leave her uneasy. She no longer trusts her own judgment, because in her mind she has already seen what her judgment can cost.

Her memory of the event does not stay in the past. Something in the environment can bring it back in full before she has time to prepare. A stretch of sidewalk near an intersection, the screech of brakes outside the parish office, sunlight falling a certain way across pavement—these can pull her abruptly into the scene. At such moments it is not a general recollection but a complete return of the clearest fragments: exactly where she was standing, exactly what she saw. The vividness frightens her, especially because it can happen while she is doing something routine, such as walking from the convent to the school building or accompanying parishioners after Mass. She can be speaking to someone one second and inwardly back at the scene the next.

Over time, Margaret organized her life around not encountering what feels unbearable. She avoids the site of the event altogether, even when doing so complicates ordinary responsibilities. If there is an errand in that part of town, she asks another sister to go or invents a practical reason to take a longer route. Within the convent she also steers away from reminders of the sister who died. She lingers less in spaces they used to share, leaves quickly if conversation turns to her, and has found reasons not to sort old belongings or look through commemorative materials. These are not casual preferences; to Margaret, such reminders feel dangerous, as though opening herself to them would unleash the worst moments with full force.

She has also developed private mental rituals that she experiences as necessary. Before other sisters leave the convent, or when she knows someone is traveling, she silently repeats particular prayers and phrases in a fixed order until they feel “done right.” If she is interrupted, she starts again. She does not describe this as superstition so much as a responsibility. Some part of her feels that if she lets the sequence slip, another terrible loss could occur. She recognizes that this sounds unreasonable, yet she cannot shake the sense that vigilance must now include these acts of mental prevention.

The cost has become visible in her work and community life. As a nun, her vocation depends on presence—showing up for others, accompanying grief, moving through shared ritual—but Margaret has grown more constrained and removed. Other sisters have noticed that she declines tasks outside the convent more often and becomes tense when plans involve the area where the death occurred. Her husband is not part of this story because she is not married; instead, the closest relationships affected are those within her religious community, where her withdrawal has made her feel both guilty and increasingly alone.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a single new event but the realization that years had passed and she was still arranging her world around that day. Recently, while walking near the parish parking lot, a sudden sound of tires made the whole memory slam back into place so vividly that she had to stop where she was, unable for a moment to remember what she had been on her way to do. It frightened her that the past could overtake her so completely. She is seeking help now because she does not want to keep living as if one failure defines her entire capacity to care for others. At the same time, what frightens her most is the possibility that if she loosens her guard—if she stops avoiding, stops repeating the prayers, stops blaming herself—she will be failing the sister she lost all over again.
